candidates.title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
candidates.author: Frontier Red Team (no individual byline on page)
candidates.what_changed: Anthropic shortens its CVD disclosure window from 90 to 30 days (high/critical) and 45 days (other) for reports made on/after 2027-01-01; escalation to external coordinator after 15 days (was 30) of no maintainer response; full technical details 30 days after patch (was 45).
candidates.mechanism: Policy change justified by AI-driven vulnerability rediscovery: models find bugs faster and a bug one model finds is increasingly found by another, so 90-day secrecy assumptions no longer hold. 7-day window for actively exploited bugs unchanged. Exceptions negotiated for hard-to-deploy software (critical infrastructure) and spec/RFC-level flaws. Does not apply to un-reviewed AI findings such as OSS Scanner output.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor policy statement; claim of 'higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery' is asserted without numbers.
candidates.relevance: High for maintainers and security teams: if you maintain OSS or receive Anthropic reports, patch SLAs effectively shrink to 30/45 days from Jan 2027; overdue 90+ day high/critical reports get an extra 30 days then publication on Anthropic's dashboard.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 covered Anthropic 'Building strong safety evaluations' (Nov 13) and Cloudflare AI pentest orchestrators; this is a new, distinct item but shares the 'AI speeds up offense/defense' theme.
candidates.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team says frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities, so it is cutting its CVD window from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues and 45 days for all others, applying to vulnerabilities reported on or after January 1, 2027 (in-progress reports keep existing deadlines). Two related changes: escalation to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond, and waiting 30 days instead of 45 after a patch before publishing full technical details. Already-overdue high/critical reports (>90 days, undisclosed) get an extra 30 days, then publication on Anthropic's dashboard in line with the new policy from Jan 1, 2027. Rationale: older norms assumed human-speed fixes and unlikely independent rediscovery; 'neither assumption holds today' and Anthropic is 'seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery'. Seven-day window for actively exploited vulns unchanged. Hard cases (critical infrastructure, spec/RFC changes) get negotiated timelines. Policy excludes AI-discovered findings without human review (e.g., OSS Scanner). Mitigations for maintainers: actionable guidance plus patch/mitigation with each report, agreed pacing before sending large volumes; programs: OSS Scanner (no-cost periodic scanning for critical OSS), Claude for Open Source Program (six months of Claude Ultra free for eligible maintainers), Cyber Verification Program (tailored safeguards for defensive work).

candidates.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
candidates.author: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Zixiao Chen, Jeevana Priya Inala, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao (listed as authors on page)
candidates.organization: Microsoft Research (with UC Berkeley, Microsoft Security)
candidates.what_changed: Open-source plugin (github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer) that learns from a coding agent's past sessions in a repo to cut token cost without modifying the agent or model.
candidates.mechanism: After each session it parses the log and applies three mechanisms via existing agent interfaces: (1) micro-skills: one-line repo-specific notes added to starting context only after several sessions confirm a pattern, retired if contradicted; (2) tool pruning: drops tools history says won't be used, always keeping core run/edit tools, restorable; (3) failure-loop intervention: judge model decides if agent is stuck; if so, injects a short redirect note, then alerts the developer rather than stopping. Savings are reported net of its own model calls. Runs locally, no API key of its own.
candidates.evidence_quality: Research measurement (paper + code) by the authors on SWE-Bench, Web-Bench and security-audit tasks; not independently replicated.
candidates.relevance: Very high: drop-in cost control for Claude Code and other coding agents; profiling numbers alone (30% repeated tool calls, 16 of 23 tools never used, failed tasks = 32% of spend) are directly checkable in your own logs.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: None with Edition 1 (Anthropic agent-memory/dreaming post was Nov 6 and not in Edition 1 list). Thematically adjacent to LangChain proactive-agent memory post.
candidates.summary: Profiling Claude Code on 60 SWE-Bench tasks run in sequence per repo found three wastes: after >=5 completed tasks in a repo, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repo (only 7% matched other repos' history); the agent received 23 tool descriptions every turn but 16 were never called; the 17% of tasks that failed consumed 32% of spend. Three existing open-source cost-saving plugins each helped in some repos but not others. TokenEconomizer (UC Berkeley, MSR, Microsoft Security) adds micro-skills, tool pruning, and failure-loop intervention (judge model + redirect note + developer alert). Evaluation: 277 SWE-Bench tasks across six repos, five agent/model combinations, starting from zero history: mean cost per task down 18.4–30.9%; 'saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss'; Pass@1 rose in four of five combos. Lowering reasoning effort saved similar or more but degraded performance substantially. Early tasks can cost more while it learns, but cumulative cost fell below default in every repo by the sixth task (Claude Code). Each mechanism saves on its own; combined is best. Web-Bench (sequential web dev): 16.0–21.2% lower cost; security auditing (new repo each task): 6.4–19.6% lower. Paper: 'TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents'. Code: https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer; project: https://tokeneconomizer.github.io.

candidates.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
candidates.author: UNVERIFIED (author block not rendered by reader)
candidates.what_changed: Published three composable context-management patterns (with companion GitHub code) for agents handling multi-megabyte JSON: S3 artifact offload with content-addressed refs, on-demand result paging, dictionary descriptor compaction.
candidates.mechanism: Strategy 1: dehydrate_state()/hydrate_state() keep only lightweight refs in AgentCore memory; heavy payloads go to an S3ArtifactStore keyed by SHA-256 of canonical JSON (idempotent writes, in-process cache). Strategy 2: tool results over a sample-size threshold are stored and replaced with {_oversized, _result_handle, total, sample}; model calls get_result_page_tool(handle, offset, limit). Strategy 3: oversized dicts become a descriptor (lists -> count+5-item sample, nested dicts -> key count, scalars inline) with a handle; fallback when serialized content exceeds _MAX_TOOL_CONTENT_CHARS. Built with LangGraph on AgentCore.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor/customer measurement on their own agent (same question set before/after, measured in AgentCore Observability); not independent.
candidates.relevance: Very high: framework-agnostic pattern for any agent with huge tool outputs; code snippets are copyable.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 covered AWS Switchyard/AgentCore startup/Bedrock cost attribution; this is a different, concrete context-engineering post.
candidates.summary: Flightscape's Training Schedule Optimization agent (40+ tools, multi-MB request/response/validation JSON) had average latency >15 s; a single tool response could exceed 80,000 tokens. Three fixes: (1) persist lightweight state, offload heavy artifacts to S3 with content-addressed SHA-256 keys so re-serialized unchanged payloads aren't re-uploaded; (2) page large lists on demand: return total count, small sample and handle; model fetches slices via get_result_page_tool; (3) compact oversized dicts into structural descriptors with a handle. Results: 5-question conversation total tokens ~289,500 -> ~82,900 (~71% drop), average trace latency 15.4 s -> 3.1 s (~80%); across 100 sample questions tokens 23.6M -> 8.5M (64%) and latency 7,930 ms -> 2,461 ms (69%). Heaviest single query: input tokens ~32,000 -> ~8,000 (75%), output ~2,800 -> 477 (83%), turn latency ~165 s -> 9.9 s (94%). Full payloads remain retrievable via handles, so capability is preserved. Prereqs: Bedrock, S3 bucket, AgentCore memory, LangGraph, Python 3.12+.

candidates.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
candidates.author: UNVERIFIED (author block not rendered by reader)
candidates.what_changed: New KV_AWARE RoutingStrategy for SageMaker real-time endpoints that routes each request to the instance holding the longest actually-cached prompt match, weighted against load.
candidates.mechanism: vLLM container publishes KV cache store/evict events (enabled via SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG); SageMaker maintains a managed index of truncated one-way hashes -> instance (no prompts/tokens/tensors stored); endpoint tokenizes the prompt, looks up longest match, skips busy candidates, falls back to LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS behavior. Contrasts with PREFIX_AWARE (hash of first PrefixLength bytes/chars, blind to evictions and short early multi-turn requests).
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor benchmark (Llama 3.1 70B, 7x ml.p5.48xlarge); reproducible notebook offered; not independently confirmed.
candidates.relevance: High for teams self-hosting LLMs on SageMaker with multi-turn chat/RAG; also a good explainer on prefix-aware vs cache-state-aware routing applicable to vLLM/Dynamo generally.
candidates.summary: Four routing strategies now: RANDOM (default), LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS, PREFIX_AWARE, KV_AWARE (new). Prefix-aware fails when (a) instances evict cache but router keeps sending there, (b) early multi-turn requests are shorter than PrefixLength so turns scatter. KV-aware uses container-reported cache state. Benchmark: Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge, 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users, multi-turn chat and doc Q&A, prompts up to ~64K tokens: vs random routing, p50 TTFT down up to 97%, throughput up to 234%, KV cache hit rate from 3–48% to 80–93%. Overhead: a few ms for short prompts, more for long (mostly tokenization; tokens are passed to the model so not tokenized twice); prefix-aware overhead was 1.3–1.9 ms in part 1. Requirements: AWS vLLM DLC with vLLM 0.33.0+ (or Amazon Linux build server-sagemaker-cuda-v2.8.0+), prefix caching on, SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG set (SageMaker doesn't set it); >=2 instances or >=2 inference component copies; OpenAI-compatible Completions/Chat payloads; no bidirectional stream; AWS CLI 2.35.6+/Boto3 1.43.31+ for hit-rate observability. Gotchas: ignores prefix-aware multi-tenant isolation header and prompt_cache_key; non-null cache_salt -> 400; fallbacks are not reported in console/metrics at launch. Advice: start with prefix-aware, then A/B KV_AWARE on your traffic comparing TTFT, throughput, hit rate. Put shared content first and in stable order.

candidates.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
candidates.author: UNVERIFIED
candidates.what_changed: Guidance post with a three-question decision flow for whether each workflow step needs a model at all.
candidates.mechanism: Ask in order: can a rule check success (format/schema/keyword/range; use a fast path if partial)? can a model write the rule once (regex/JSON schema, reviewed and committed)? does the step pick from a fixed list (use a constrained decision call: small model with enum structured output + 'unsure' escalation, embedding nearest-neighbor with threshold, Strands Decider with calibrated confidence, or trained classifier)? Otherwise use the smallest right-sized model.
candidates.evidence_quality: Opinion/guidance; one cited claim from Strands Decider README (>=0.9 confidence ~95% correct on short classification) explicitly flagged to validate.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: practical checklist teams can apply to any pipeline; AWS-specific mapping (API Gateway validation, Step Functions JSONata Choice, Lambda, Bedrock).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: None with Edition 1 (adjacent to Bedrock cost attribution theme).
candidates.summary: Argues the biggest cost lever is whether to call a model at all; prototypes default every step (validation, reformatting, routing) to an LLM, which at production volume adds spend, stacked latency (hundreds of ms per call), and nondeterminism. Worked example of a support assistant: order-number format check -> API Gateway validation/Lambda; intent routing -> keyword fast path in Step Functions Choice (JSONata) plus constrained decision call for residual; tracking-number extraction -> model-written regex committed to Lambda; queue selection -> constrained decision call with escalation; reply drafting -> smallest adequate Bedrock model. Table contrasting code vs model on cost, latency (single-digit ms vs hundreds of ms), correctness, auditability, stability across model versions. Notes temperature 0 doesn't guarantee identical output. Includes a JSON schema limiting answers to four queues plus 'unsure' (Bedrock requires additionalProperties:false on every object). Mentions Strands Decider (experimental Apache-2.0 decision model) whose README claims answers at confidence >=0.9 are right ~95% on short classification; warns to validate.

candidates.title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
candidates.author: UNVERIFIED
candidates.what_changed: HyperPod Inference add-on now installs and manages NVIDIA Dynamo for multi-node, disaggregated prefill/decode serving with KV-aware routing and fault recovery.
candidates.mechanism: Add-on installs Dynamo CRDs plus HyperPod Inference Operator (InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec), Dynamo operator (DynamoGraphDeployment), Grove (pod-group coordination), KAI Scheduler (gang scheduling). Two paths: bring-your-own DGD, or IEC dynamoSpec with operator-managed weights staging from S3/FSx, TLS/registration, KEDA autoscaling. Engines: vLLM (default), SGLang, TensorRT-LLM. routingMode: kv-aware.
candidates.evidence_quality: Product announcement with configuration examples; no benchmark numbers captured.
candidates.relevance: Medium: for teams serving very large open models (example GLM-5.3 FP8 exceeds 640 GB on one p5.48xlarge) on Kubernetes.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 covered NVIDIA GLM-5.3 on DGX Stations; different deployment target.
candidates.summary: Motivation: GLM-5.3 FP8 weights exceed the 640 GB GPU memory of one ml.p5.48xlarge before KV cache; long prompts slow generation on shared GPUs. Dynamo supports multi-node, disaggregated prefill/decode (separately scalable pools, KV transfer between them), aggregated serving, tensor/pipeline parallelism, and a KV-aware router weighing prefix reuse and worker load. HyperPod handles node/GPU/EFA health and replacement. Example: one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs) with two frontend replicas; dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode: kv-aware.

candidates.title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
candidates.author: UNVERIFIED
candidates.what_changed: Field taxonomy splitting multi-agent patterns into Tier 1 (deterministic control flow) and Tier 2 (LLM-determined control flow), plus five budget-burning anti-patterns.
candidates.mechanism: Decision rule: if you can draw the control flow on a whiteboard before runtime, use Tier 1; move to Tier 2 only when subtasks are discovered during work. Anti-pattern fixes: hard iteration ceiling in code, per-agent token ceiling, budget alarm wired to automatic stop; prefer one agent with tool groups over many 'specialists' (gains flatten around four agents). Debate pattern is most expensive and buys latency not accuracy on perceptual tasks.
candidates.evidence_quality: Opinion/field experience; cites external stats (~88% of pilots never reach production; Stanford HAI collaboration finding) without independent verification here.
candidates.relevance: Medium: useful architecture checklist; manufacturing specifics (takt time, edge data 50+ GB/day per press, shift cycles) less general.
candidates.summary: Frames multi-agent coordination as a distributed-systems problem. Reliability compounding: ten 95%-reliable steps yield ~59.9% end-to-end. Tier 1 patterns (sequential pipeline, etc.) are debuggable with predictable cost; Tier 2 (autonomous orchestration, debate, plan-based) add tokens, latency, debugging burden. Anti-patterns include unbounded 'try again' retry loops (fix: infrastructure-enforced limits, 'the model will not stop itself') and multi-agent where a single agent with tool groups would do (non-linear coordination tax). Recommends tiered model selection (small model for router classification, stronger for orchestrator synthesis), context compression, edge-cloud split. Exact list of all five anti-patterns not fully captured: UNVERIFIED.

candidates.title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
candidates.author: Trammell Saltzgaber
candidates.what_changed: LangSmith Enterprise adds three trace-access controls: hide trace inputs/outputs per user, user groups with per-workspace permissions, and trace-level ABAC policies keyed on root run metadata.
candidates.mechanism: Send full-fidelity traces once; admins restrict who sees inputs/outputs while engineers still see run trees, latency, cost, token usage. Groups layer on existing RBAC/ABAC. Metadata policies (e.g., customer_id, user_id on root run) grant per-trace access, avoiding duplicate redacted workspaces.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor feature announcement; no metrics.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high for teams with PII/HIPAA traces: design pattern (tag root runs with tenant/user IDs, separate content from telemetry access) applies beyond LangSmith. Enterprise plan only.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: None with Edition 1 (Edition 1 covered LangChain Goal Engineering).
candidates.summary: Problem: production traces contain names, health info, payment details subject to GDPR/HIPAA/CCPA and contracts (ISO 27001, SOC 2), forcing teams to either duplicate traces across workspaces or not trace at all. New controls: (1) restrict trace inputs/outputs (user messages, model responses) so engineers debug from run trees, perf stats, metadata; (2) user groups with per-workspace permissions layered on RBAC/ABAC (e.g., clinicians see I/O for annotation, engineers see only run trees/latency/tokens); (3) trace-level ABAC policies from root run metadata (support agents see only their customers' traces; developers only their own coding-agent traces). Combined: store complete traces once, no redacted copies; change a team's customer scope by editing the metadata policy. Available on LangSmith Enterprise plans.

candidates.title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
candidates.author: Sydney Runkle
candidates.what_changed: Lessons from LangChain's internal proactive agents (GTM Agent and Robin, formerly Open SWE) on triggers, memory and check-in UX.
candidates.mechanism: Three trigger sources: real-world events, developer-set schedules, agent-set schedules. Memory from seed (past), feedback (present), outcomes (future); maintenance problems: salience, expiry, duplication, often handled by a scheduled 'dreaming' job over recent traces. UX: high signal (decision model 'Jev' decides when Robin joins Slack threads), built for fast review, live where users work (Slack, headline + threaded detail).
candidates.evidence_quality: Practitioner experience; one internal metric (>70% of Managed Deep Agents runs come from schedules).
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: concrete design checklist for background agents; suggested metric: share of check-ins the user acts on, draft approval time.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Overlaps theme with Edition 1's LangChain Goal Engineering; cites it directly. Adds new practitioner detail.
candidates.summary: Proactive agents run in background toward goals and decide when to check in; attention is the scarce resource. Examples: GTM Agent (watches leads, daily briefs, drafts outbound email) and Robin (drafts and reviews every PR). Built on Managed Deep Agents, where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than ad hoc prompts. Memory signals: seed (e.g., sent folder), feedback (rewrites/rejections), outcomes (replies received). Hard parts: salience, expiry, duplication; 'dreaming' scheduled job updates memory from traces. Measure memory via outcomes: draft approval time, reply rate, share of check-ins acted on. UX: GTM Agent's review UI sorts conversations into waiting-on-you / needs-draft / no-reply; Robin uses Jev as a decision model for when to join Slack conversations; one-to-two-sentence headline with details in thread; PR review requests with one-line summary, change size and a claim button; custom UI built because Slack review of email backlogs was slow. Build with Managed Deep Agents (schedules, memory, async subagents) or open-source Deep Agents (JS too).

candidates.title: We rebuilt LangSmith around the agent
candidates.author: Sam Crowder
candidates.what_changed: LangSmith re-organized around an 'agent record' (owner, immutable ID, type) grouping traces, environments, evals, Agent Server and Engine issues; agent types (general purpose, coding with GitHub connection) give opinionated dashboards; OTLP ingestion registers agents from any platform.
candidates.mechanism: Replaces flat project hierarchy with one agent record holding local/dev/staging/prod environments under the same ID; types determine dashboard, data connections, eval criteria (coding: merged PRs, token cost, work type). Agent registry + LLM Gateway for governance; cost/quality roll up per agent with a named owner.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor product post; no metrics.
candidates.relevance: Medium: governance pattern (every agent has owner/ID/type, OTLP-registered) is a useful idea for platform teams regardless of vendor.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to LangChain Series C (Nov 13) and Edition 1 LangChain coverage; distinct product detail.
candidates.summary: Rationale: companies run many agents across frameworks/runtimes; engineers context-switch between tracing, monitoring, deployments and skip evals; platform teams can't answer which agents exist, owners, costs. New model: build (natural-language builder in LangSmith Studio or code), run (Agent Server or own runtime), improve (tracing, evals, datasets, annotation, Engine), govern (agent registry, LLM Gateway). Engine can validate a proposed fix against an Agent Server preview before merge. Works with any OTLP-capable platform including vendor agents (examples: ServiceNow, Glean). Roadmap: Engine red-teaming and regression monitoring, custom annotation apps feeding eval datasets, fine-tuning from best trajectories, voice agent type, org-level dashboards, registering agents in identity providers. Available in cloud, BYOC, self-hosted.

candidates.title: From tasks to goals
candidates.author: Harrison Chase
candidates.what_changed: Essay listing practical requirements when agents are given goals rather than tasks.
candidates.mechanism: Six shifts each with a 'practical consideration': agent chooses tasks (visible to-do list, prompting for varied task brainstorming); unknown tool calls (tighter tool allow/deny controls); inbox for clarifying questions; feedback mechanism tied to metrics plus human correction; triggers (heartbeats, recurring cron, one-off cron, event streams) plus stopping rules ('sometimes doing nothing is the right action'); memory so feedback compounds across runs.
candidates.evidence_quality: Opinion essay.
candidates.relevance: Medium: checklist for goal-driven agents.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Strong overlap with Edition 1's LangChain Goal Engineering coverage (Nov 14 post); likely skip or fold in as a line.
candidates.summary: Goals specify an outcome and an ongoing responsibility rather than an action and bounded assignment. The agent must decompose into tasks and be creatively varied; you need to see its task list. Tool needs are unknown up front so you need controls over callable tools. Background agents need a way to ask humans (Slack or dedicated UI). Progress feedback: metrics plus explicit human feedback; design goals so feedback is easy. Wake mechanisms: heartbeats every X minutes, recurring cron, one-off cron reminders, event streams, plus ability to stop/pause/ignore triggers to avoid repeat pings. Memory carries decisions forward (rejecting a blog topic should inform future topic selection).

candidates.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
candidates.author: Célina Hanouti, Victor Mustar, Bertrand Chevrier, Lucain Pouget, Pierric Cistac, Eliott Coyac, Julien Chaumond
candidates.what_changed: HF Inference Providers switched from its own router to OpenRouter's for language models: per-request provider selection on live price/speed/reliability, automatic retry on another provider, cache-aware stickiness. Breaking change: custom provider API keys no longer work for LLMs.
candidates.mechanism: Model-id suffixes select policy/provider (:fastest, :cheapest, :<provider>); X-HF-Session-Id header with a stable UUID per conversation keeps it on the provider holding the prompt cache; providers can be disabled per user/org; router supports OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic Messages API for every chat model; setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Hermes Agent. No HF markup; PRO gets $2/month credits.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor announcement; routing improvement numbers are OpenRouter's own measurements; usage-share numbers cite OpenRouter data.
candidates.relevance: High: anyone calling HF Inference Providers with their own provider keys must change setup; easy way to point coding agents at open-weight models via an Anthropic-compatible endpoint.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: None with Edition 1 (Edition 1 covered llama.cpp 1.0 and XYBench on HF).
candidates.summary: Every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves is callable with an HF token through one API, with OpenRouter routing across 80+ providers. OpenRouter's rebuilt routing (best mix of price, speed, reliability; traffic moves off failing providers; failed tries retried within the same call) cut capacity errors 46%, improved TTFT 16.9% and throughput 16.3% (OpenRouter measurements). Examples: zai-org/GLM-5.3 (default), :fastest, :cheapest, :novita. Open-weight share of OpenRouter tokens: 26.8% (Oct 2025) -> 71.7% (end Sep 2026), peak 77.5% July; weekly open-weight volume grew >60x vs ~10x closed. Most-used model this week: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, 59.2T tokens. Average prices: open $0.28/M in, $1.62/M out vs closed $1.27 and $6.36. AA Intelligence Index: Kimi K3.1 Pro 46 vs Claude Fable 5.2 65 at ~1/7 cost per task ($3.68 vs $26.54). OpenRouter: 800T+ tokens/month, 10M+ users, 600+ models. Image/video/audio generation unchanged (not via OpenRouter); custom keys for image/video still work. Model pages get Providers and Metrics tabs; usage overview breaks spend by provider.

candidates.title: How we optimized our workflows and overcame GitHub Actions limitations
candidates.author: Georgi Gerganov, merve (ggml-org)
candidates.what_changed: llama.cpp moved CI compiler caches (ccache) to Hugging Face Buckets and most Linux x64 jobs to Hugging Face Jobs via jobs-actions, and split PR vs master workflows with diff-based job selection.
candidates.mechanism: ccache snapshots uploaded to an HF Bucket after eligible master builds; PR builds download snapshot. jobs-actions: GitHub queues a job with an hf-jobs-* runs-on label -> signed webhook to a dispatcher Space -> verifies, mints short-lived runner registration token -> starts an HF Job that boots an ephemeral GitHub runner, executes, reports, exits.
candidates.evidence_quality: Project write-up; no before/after CI timing numbers captured.
candidates.relevance: Medium: reusable recipe for large OSS repos hitting GitHub's 10 GB cache and 20-concurrent-job free-plan limits.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 covered llama.cpp 1.0; this is a separate infra post.
candidates.summary: Scale: Aug–Oct 2026 llama.cpp received 3,181 PRs (~35/day), merged 1,802; full CI is 100+ jobs, many up to ~30 min; pre-release builds for most master merges. Limits: GitHub Actions cache 10 GB for free public repos (LRU eviction forced recompiles, painful for template-heavy CUDA/HIP/MUSA builds); free plan 20 concurrent hosted jobs org-wide, max five macOS. candidates.title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference
candidates.author: Timmy Liu, Nidhi Bhatia, Samkit Jain, Makesh Tarun Chandran, Bita Darvish Rouhani
candidates.what_changed: Kernel-level design guidelines for sparse-attention indexers and Top-k selection (DeepSeek DSA, GLM 5.2/5.3 Flash, LongCat LSA-Flash, MiniMax MSA, etc.), plus fused Top-k in TensorRT LLM.
candidates.mechanism: Sparse attention = indexer scores all N keys, Top-k keeps k, core attention over k. Indexer cost grows with N so it dominates at long context. Guidelines include: keep G x (D+1) within one Tensor Core tile (~200 rows, 256 with FP16 epilogue); decode cost scales linearly with key heads; reduce keys scored via compression, hierarchical indexing, index sharing; fuse Top-k into indexer to avoid logit write/read-back; Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k reuses previous decode step's selection.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor microbenchmarks; code in TensorRT LLM.
candidates.relevance: Medium (inference engineers/model architects); low for app developers.
candidates.summary: At 128K tokens dense attention can take most of a layer's prefill time. Measurements: decode runtime moves only 2% while query group size G grows 16x (key cache read dominates); prefill doubling G 8->16 costs 1.66x; with an FP32 epilogue one pass can score G x (D+1) up to ~200 rows (six query tokens at G=32, 26 at G=8) with runtime up only 1.37x/1.87x for 6x/26x work; FP16 epilogue gives 1.31x at G=64, D+1=4; FP16 accumulation 1.45x if outputs stay in range. Key heads: decode runtime 7.6x from KH=1 to 8; prefill 1.3–1.6x. Head size 64->128 costs only 1.1–1.2x in prefill. Top-k: each doubling of scored keys ~1.7x prefill/1.5x decode, but 64x more k raises Top-k time under 2x. Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k in TensorRT LLM is 2.1–2.4x faster than standard radix select on DeepSeek V3.2/V4 decode. Block-level selection shares fetches across queries.

candidates.title: How we raised Databricks cluster rate limits by 7.5×
candidates.author: Heqing Ya, Tan Zhang, Ankit Batra, Abhishek Rai
candidates.what_changed: Databricks replaced fixed request-rate limits on cluster creation with adaptive concurrency limits, bounded queues and fair scheduling, keeping a fixed API rate cap as a last guardrail.
candidates.mechanism: Each long-running provisioning workflow holds a slot until done (not a thread); slot limit adapts to health signals (provisioning duration, thread-pool saturation); bounded queue with per-request deadlines and cheap expiry; tenant-fair scheduling; separate metrics for system degradation vs tenant excess demand; retries need backoff and attempt caps to avoid retry storms.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor-reported rollout results 'in the reported scope'.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high for anyone throttling long-running agent/tool jobs or LLM batch work: the rate-vs-concurrency distinction and retry-storm warning transfer directly.
candidates.summary: Fixed request-rate limits fail for long-running ops: they reject work when capacity is spare and keep accepting when dependencies slow (work in flight grows with duration); internal retries from accepted work are invisible to the API limiter and cause retry storms. Solution: slots per active cluster-creation workflow, adaptive slot count from health signals, bounded queue that only holds work that can still meet its deadline, inexpensive queued records and bulk expiry, explicit fairness policy (100 customers each one slow request vs one customer 100 slow). Rollout results: 7.5x higher default cluster-creation request-rate limits; >99.99% fewer cluster-creation rate-limit errors in reported scope; over a hundred customer-specific overrides removed; no new manual overrides since. Future: weighted slots for heterogeneous costs, control placement across multiple bottlenecks.

candidates.title: Built on object storage, served from cache
candidates.author: Carlota Soto
candidates.what_changed: Production read-tier stats for Lakebase Postgres (Neon-style compute/pageserver/safekeeper architecture on object storage).
candidates.mechanism: Tiered reads: compute local cache -> pageserver NVMe (GetPage@LSN, LSM of image/delta layers) -> object storage; each tier caches what it fetches.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor production telemetry on 'a slice of our production fleet'.
candidates.relevance: Low for AI practitioners (database infra); relevant only to teams using Lakebase for agent state.
candidates.summary: Fleet slice: compute local cache ~1.1 billion page accesses/s (~99.46%); pageserver NVMe ~6 million reads/s (~0.54%); object storage ~39 requests/s, i.e., ~1 in 28 million accesses (>99.99999% served without object storage). Object-store reads are mainly wakeups of long-dormant projects, restores or old branches. Durability via S3 (11 nines), branching/restores as metadata ops, scale-to-zero compute, LTAP (one copy for transactions and analytics). Safekeepers replicate WAL with Paxos-based quorum.
